papers.title: Flow Map Language Models: One-step Language Modeling via Continuous Denoising

papers.why: Splicing-derived immunotherapy targets; filtering normal-tissue isoforms.

papers.why: Jes: normalizing-flow based SBI.

papers.title: The alternative splicing of tau exon 10 and its regulatory proteins CLK2 and TRA2-BETA1 changes in sporadic Alzheimer's disease

papers.title: Adaptive Cholesky Gaussian Processes
papers.why: Jes/Hauberg: cheaper exact GP inference by stopping Cholesky early.

papers.title: The Multivariate Generalised von Mises distribution: Inference and applications
papers.why: Jes: distributions on the torus, e.g. protein dihedral angles.

papers.title: VampPrior Unleashed
papers.why: Upgrades the VampPrior (decoupled prior/posterior covariances, Dirichlet-process weights) and plugs it into scVI — directly relevant to your hierarchical single-cell latent models.

papers.title: Large Flow Language Models (Lafa)
papers.why: Shows continuous blockwise flows can be scaled to 8B-parameter language models by adapting AR models — a reference point for continuous vs discrete generation of sequences.

papers.title: Ch. 1–2: Introduction and making maps
papers.why: Why geometry at all: latent spaces of generative models are not identifiable, so distances measured there are arbitrary. The map-making analogy sets up the whole book, and it matters every time you interpret an scVI-style latent space.

papers.title: Ch. 1–2.2: Machine learning on graphs, statistics and kernels
papers.why: The graph learning tasks (node, edge and graph level) and the classic hand-built features and kernels. A quick foundation; splice graphs and gene-regulatory networks are both graph data close to your work.

papers.title: Ch. 3: Embedded and immersed manifolds
papers.why: Manifold learning as reparametrisation, statistical identifiability, and the embedded vs immersed distinction the rest of the book relies on.

papers.title: Ch. 2.3–2.4: Graph Laplacians and spectral methods
papers.why: The graph Laplacian, graph cuts and spectral clustering. The Laplacian is also the generator of diffusion on a graph, a direct bridge to CTMCs and discrete diffusion.

papers.title: Ch. 4: Distances on manifolds
papers.why: Curve lengths and why they are invariant to reparametrisation: the core argument for measuring in data space instead of latent space.

papers.title: Ch. 3: Node embeddings by neighbourhood reconstruction
papers.why: The encoder–decoder view, matrix factorisation and random-walk embeddings (DeepWalk, node2vec), and why shallow embeddings are limited.

papers.title: Ch. 5–6: Riemannian metrics and learned metrics
papers.why: The central chapter: tangent spaces, local inner products, the pull-back metric JᵀJ, and metrics learned from densities, autoencoders and classifiers. This is the language behind Riemannian flow matching and Fisher–Rao geometry on the simplex.

papers.title: Ch. 5.1–5.2: Message passing and neighbourhood aggregation
papers.why: The core GNN: message passing, normalisation, set aggregators and attention. The basis for the equivariant GNNs (EGNN) on your protein track.

papers.title: Ch. 7: Geodesics
papers.why: Curve energy and the geodesic ODE. Geodesics are the 'straight lines' that Riemannian flow matching and Riemannian score models interpolate along.

papers.title: Ch. 5.3–5.6: Updates, edge features and pooling
papers.why: Skip and gated updates, relational GNNs, graph pooling and generalised message passing.

papers.title: Ch. 8: Computing geodesics numerically (+ appendix on ODEs)
papers.why: Direct length minimisation vs shooting geodesics. The short appendix on Euler's method and Picard–Lindelöf is the same toolkit as ODE samplers for flows.

papers.title: Ch. 7.1: GNNs and graph convolutions
papers.why: From the Fourier transform to spectral graph convolutions, and why GCNs act as low-pass filters on the graph.

papers.title: Ch. 9–10: Arithmetic and integration on manifolds
papers.why: Exp and log maps, means on manifolds, volume measures and densities. What you need to define probability densities and expectations on curved spaces, as manifold flow and diffusion models do.

papers.title: Ch. 7.2–7.3: GNNs, graphical models and the WL test
papers.why: GNNs as embedded mean-field inference, and the expressiveness limits set by the Weisfeiler–Lehman test. Links GNNs back to the probabilistic models of your group.

papers.title: Ch. 11–12.3: Submanifolds and noisy manifolds
papers.why: Composite maps, ambient metrics and manifolds observed through noise: the realistic setting for learned data manifolds.

papers.title: Ch. 8–9.1: Graph generation: classic models and VAEs
papers.why: Erdős–Rényi, stochastic block models and preferential attachment, then graph VAEs with node- and graph-level latents.

papers.title: Ch. 12.4: Statistical submanifolds
papers.why: Families of distributions as manifolds with the Fisher information metric, i.e. information geometry. Directly relevant to isoform proportions on the simplex, where Fisher–Rao geometry is the sphere geometry used by Fisher flow matching.

papers.title: Ch. 9.2–9.5: Autoregressive graph generation and molecules
papers.why: Adversarial and autoregressive graph generators, how to evaluate them, and molecule generation. A springboard to graph diffusion (e.g. DiGress) if you want to go further.

papers.title: Ch. 14–15: Parameter manifolds and further reading
papers.why: Metrics on network parameters (function-space and information metrics, overparametrisation), then Hauberg's own guide to where to go next.

papers.title: Ch. 4: Multi-relational data and knowledge graphs
papers.why: Embedding typed relations. Background if you ever combine gene, isoform and protein relations in one graph; lower priority.

papers.title: Ch. 6: GNNs in practice
papers.why: Loss functions, mini-batching, neighbourhood sampling and regularisation when training GNNs.

papers.title: Ch. 13: Expected Gaussian manifolds
papers.why: Manifolds defined by Gaussian-process decoders: expected metrics, energies and lengths. A probabilistic treatment of uncertainty in learned geometry; deeper and optional on a first pass.

papers.title: UDL Ch. 5: Loss functions
papers.why: Maximum likelihood as the recipe for every loss: Gaussian → least squares, Bernoulli → binary cross-entropy, categorical → softmax cross-entropy. Students often treat losses as arbitrary; this chapter is where the probabilistic view you use daily is introduced.

papers.title: UDL Ch. 6: Fitting models
papers.why: Gradient descent, SGD, momentum and Adam, with learning-rate and batch-size intuition. Expect student questions on why Adam 'just works' and on choosing learning rates.

papers.title: UDL Ch. 7: Gradients and initialization
papers.why: Backpropagation from scratch and He/Xavier initialisation via variance of activations. The classic place students get lost; the toy example is worth working through by hand.

papers.title: UDL Ch. 10: Convolutional networks
papers.why: Invariance vs equivariance, 1D and 2D convolutions, stride, padding, dilation, pooling and upsampling. Shape bookkeeping (channels, receptive fields) is the usual project stumbling block.

papers.title: Goodfellow Ch. 10.1–10.2: Recurrent networks and BPTT
papers.why: Unfolding computational graphs, RNN variants, teacher forcing, backpropagation through time and RNNs as directed graphical models. Read before the transformer chapter: it is the problem attention solves.

papers.title: Goodfellow Ch. 10.3–10.12: Encoder–decoders, long-term dependencies, LSTM/GRU
papers.why: Bidirectional and encoder–decoder RNNs, vanishing/exploding gradients, leaky units, gated units (LSTM, GRU), gradient clipping and explicit memory. Skim 10.6 (recursive nets) and 10.8 (echo state networks) if short on time.

papers.title: UDL Ch. 14: Unsupervised learning
papers.why: Short chapter: a taxonomy of generative models and how to evaluate them (likelihood, FID and friends). Sets up Friday's flows and VAEs.

papers.title: UDL Ch. 12: Transformers
papers.why: Dot-product self-attention, positional encodings, multi-head attention, BERT, GPT-3, encoder–decoders and vision transformers. The chapter students will lean on most; be ready to explain Q/K/V shapes and masking.

papers.title: UDL Ch. 13: Graph neural networks
papers.why: Adjacency representations, GCNs, inductive vs transductive learning, node and graph classification, edge graphs. A compact version of Hamilton's chapters 5–7, which come later on your path.

papers.title: UDL Ch. 16: Normalizing flows
papers.why: Change of variables, invertible layers (coupling, autoregressive, residual flows), multi-scale flows. The bridge from these course chapters to continuous flows and flow matching in your own work.

papers.title: UDL Ch. 17: Variational autoencoders
papers.why: Latent variable models, the ELBO, the reparameterisation trick. Familiar ground for you; read it for how Prince presents it, since that is what your students will have seen.

papers.title: Computational Optimal Transport, Ch. 1–2: theoretical foundations
papers.why: Monge and Kantorovich problems, couplings and Wasserstein distances. Read chapters 1–2. The foundation under OT conditional flow matching and Schrödinger bridges.

papers.title: Computational Optimal Transport, Ch. 4: entropic regularization and Sinkhorn
papers.why: Entropic OT and the Sinkhorn algorithm: what minibatch OT in flow matching actually computes, and the static version of a Schrödinger bridge.

papers.title: Optimal-Transport Analysis of Single-Cell Gene Expression Identifies Developmental Trajectories in Reprogramming (Waddington-OT)
papers.why: The paper that brought OT to single-cell biology: coupling cell populations across time points to infer trajectories. A template for population-level generative questions in your data.

papers.title: Simulation-free Schrödinger bridges via score and flow matching
papers.why: Learns stochastic dynamics between distributions with entropic OT plus flow and score matching; applied to single-cell trajectories.

papers.title: Learning single-cell perturbation responses using neural optimal transport (CellOT)
papers.why: Perturbation response as an OT map between control and treated cells. Where the OT and perturbation threads meet.

papers.title: An Elementary Introduction to Information Geometry
papers.why: Fisher information metric, dual connections and exponential families, written for ML readers. Long; read the core sections on the Fisher metric and exponential/mixture families first. Turns Hauberg's statistical-manifolds chapter into a toolkit for the simplex.

papers.title: Markov Chains, Ch. 2: Continuous-time Markov chains I
papers.why: Q-matrices and their exponentials, Poisson processes, jump chain and holding times, forward and backward equations. The theory under your CTMC / generator-matching work. Some sections are previewable on Norris's page; the full book should be on Cambridge Core via DTU Library.

papers.title: Markov Chains, Ch. 3: Continuous-time Markov chains II
papers.why: Class structure, hitting times, invariant distributions, convergence to equilibrium and time reversal: what you need to reason about forward noising processes and their reversals.

papers.title: The Statistical Analysis of Compositional Data
papers.why: Log-ratio analysis of proportions on the simplex. The classical statistics answer to the question your isoform models face: how to model fractions that must sum to one.

papers.title: Microbiome Datasets Are Compositional: And This Is Not Optional
papers.why: A short, practical argument for why sequencing counts are compositional and what goes wrong otherwise. Easy read; the same logic applies to isoform counts within a gene.

papers.title: Understanding sequencing data as compositions: an outlook and review
papers.why: Review of compositional methods for sequencing data: normalisation, log-ratios, proportionality and differential abundance.

papers.title: Separating measurement and expression models clarifies confusion in single-cell RNA sequencing analysis
papers.why: Splits scRNA-seq modelling into a measurement model (Poisson / multinomial sampling) and an expression model, which settles the 'zero inflation' debate. A clean way to think about your NB + multinomial hierarchy.

papers.title: Geometric Deep Learning (proto-book), Sections 1–3: learning in high dimensions and geometric priors
papers.why: Symmetry, invariance, equivariance and scale separation as the unifying idea behind CNNs, GNNs, transformers and equivariant networks. Ties together your graph, geometry and protein tracks.

papers.title: Geometric Deep Learning (proto-book), Sections 4–5: the 5 Gs and the models
papers.why: Grids, groups, graphs, geodesics and gauges, and the architectures each one gives rise to.

papers.title: DiGress: Discrete Denoising diffusion for graph generation
papers.why: Discrete diffusion over node and edge categories with marginal-preserving noise. Discrete diffusion on structured objects, close to your lattice-simplex setting.

papers.title: Score-based Generative Modeling of Graphs via the System of Stochastic Differential Equations (GDSS)
papers.why: The continuous counterpart to DiGress: joint SDEs over node features and adjacency.

papers.title: Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, Ch. 2: Regression
papers.why: Weight-space and function-space views of GP regression, predictive distributions and the marginal likelihood. Background for Hauberg's expected Gaussian manifolds and for Bayesian work in your group.

papers.title: Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, Ch. 5: Model selection and hyperparameters
papers.why: Marginal likelihood, Occam's razor and cross-validation for kernel hyperparameters.

papers.title: scGen predicts single-cell perturbation responses
papers.why: Latent-space vector arithmetic in a VAE to predict how unseen cell types respond to perturbation. The starting point of deep perturbation modelling.

papers.title: Predicting cellular responses to complex perturbations in high-throughput screens (CPA)
papers.why: Compositional perturbation autoencoder: disentangles basal state, perturbation, dose and covariates, so combinations can be predicted.

papers.title: VAE with a VampPrior
papers.why: The original VampPrior: a mixture of variational posteriors at learned pseudo-inputs as the VAE prior — the foundation VampPrior Unleashed builds on.

papers.title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
papers.why: When does a likelihood-based flow-matching objective on a manifold recover the true marginal velocity? A clean 'compatibility' condition worth knowing for simplex/manifold flows.

papers.title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models
papers.why: Exact reward tilts by moving where the denoiser is evaluated rather than adding a drift — a natural sequel to Jeffrey guidance and the flow-matching guidance survey.

papers.title: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks
papers.authors: Casado Noguerales, von Rütte, Schölkopf, Hofmann & Raoufi
papers.why: A CTMC whose state is a candidate set per position — a different corruption kernel to compare with masked/uniform discrete diffusion and your lattice-simplex generators.

papers.title: Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
papers.why: Puts contrastive embeddings on the probability simplex with a Total Variation similarity, a light way into simplex geometry as a representation space.

papers.title: Trajectory Matching: Discrete Flow Matching with Structured Actions
papers.why: Extends discrete flow matching from endpoint-conditioned, component-wise edits to paths of structured actions — a useful contrast to your CTMC generator matching on the lattice simplex.

papers.title: Deep Sets
papers.authors: Zaheer, Kottur, Ravanbakhsh, Póczos, Salakhutdinov, Smola
papers.why: The sum-decomposition characterisation of permutation-invariant functions that the Set Transformer builds on — the basic tool for models over unordered sets of cells or isoforms.

papers.title: Set Transformer: A Framework for Attention-based Permutation-Invariant Neural Networks
papers.authors: Lee, Lee, Kim, Kosiorek, Choi, Teh
papers.why: Attention-based pooling over sets (ISAB/PMA) — a natural architecture for permutation-invariant inputs like cells or a gene's isoforms, and a direct follow-on to this week's transformer reading.

papers.title: Active Flow Expansion for Out-of-Distribution Discovery: from Theory to Molecules
papers.authors: De Santi, Lee, Perez Jensen, Protopapas, Tang, Liu, Chatterjee, Yue, Krause
papers.why: Continued pre-training that uses verifier feedback to expand a flow model's generable set beyond the data — a principled take on generating valid designs the training data never covered.

papers.title: Verifier-Constrained Flow Expansion for Discovery Beyond the Data
papers.why: Expands a pre-trained flow model's density beyond the data via verifier-constrained entropy maximisation (mirror descent) — the companion to Active Flow Expansion, with convergence guarantees.

papers.title: Provable Maximum Entropy Manifold Exploration via Diffusion Models
papers.authors: De Santi, Vlastelica, Hsieh, Shen, He, Krause
papers.why: Foundation for both Flow Expansion papers: exploration as entropy maximisation over a diffusion model's manifold, solved by mirror-descent fine-tuning using the entropy–score connection (ICML 2025).

papers.title: On the Selectivity of Generative Models in Structure-Based Drug Design
papers.authors: Rajaonson, Lee, Chau, Aspuru-Guzik, Sanchez-Lengeling, Beaini, Neklyudov, Skreta
papers.why: Read independently on 2026-11-10.

papers.title: Feynman-Kac Correctors in Diffusion: Annealing, Guidance, and Product of Experts
papers.authors: Skreta, Akhound-Sadegh, Ohanesian, Bondesan, Aspuru-Guzik, Doucet, Brekelmans, Tong, Neklyudov
papers.why: Because you read On the Selectivity of Generative Models in Structure-Based Drug Design: this is the FKC guidance method it benchmarks — SMC reweighting that makes annealing, CFG and product-of-experts sampling exact, and a natural sibling to the group's SMC-guidance work.
